lpic1-cron-at.title: An at reminder and a weekly cron cleanup
lpic1-cron-at.briefing:
You are asked to schedule two tasks for your user:
1. Use `at` to schedule a job 2 hours from now that writes the word `recordatorio` to `recordatorio.txt` (in your challenge directory). Save only the job number assigned by `at` to `at-id.txt`.
2. Schedule a similar job for 3 hours from now and cancel it with `atrm`. Only the first job should remain in the queue.
3. Save the output of `atq` to `atq.txt`: a single line, for the first job.
4. Add to your crontab, without deleting anything already there, a five-field line that runs the script `limpia.sh` from your challenge directory (with the full path) every Sunday at 04:00.
Your terminal opens in the challenge directory (`/home/alumno/retos/r102-cron-at`); the files requested without a path go there.
lpic1-cron-at.blind_alert: REQUEST [SCHEDULING] · Need to set up a one-time reminder and a weekly cleanup for your user.
hints: `at` reads the command from standard input and responds with a job number. The queue is checked and cleared with two other commands of the same family.
Try `echo 'command' | at now + 2 hours` and check the queue with `atq`. For the crontab, `crontab -l` shows what's there and `crontab -e` edits it; Sunday is 0 in the day-of-week field.

Something like: `echo 'echo recordatorio > PATH/recordatorio.txt' | at now + 2 hours`, write the number to `at-id.txt`; repeat with `3 hours` and remove that one with `atrm NUM`; then `atq > atq.txt`. The cron line starts with `0 4 * * 0`.
lpic1-cron-at.solution_summary: With `at` you schedule by piping the command to stdin (`echo '…' | at now + 2 hours`); the printed number goes to `at-id.txt`. Cancel the second job with `atrm`, and `atq > atq.txt` saves the queue with only one job. In the crontab (`crontab -e`), the line `0 4 * * 0 /path/limpia.sh` means minute 0, hour 4, any day of month, any month, Sunday.

lpic1-gpg-simetrico.title: GnuPG: password encryption, key pair, and message for a recipient
lpic1-gpg-simetrico.briefing:
You are asked to work with GnuPG without touching your `~/.gnupg`. Before starting, in the terminal:
`export GNUPGHOME=/home/alumno/retos/r102-gpg-simetrico/gnupg`
1. Encrypt `secreto.txt` with the password `clave-reto` (without `gpg` prompting) and save the result to `secreto.txt.gpg`.
2. Generate a key pair with the default values (ed25519 with an encryption subkey), no passphrase and no expiry, for `Alumno LPI <alumno@lpi.example>`, with no interactive questions.
3. Export the public key in ASCII format to `publica.asc`.
4. Encrypt `mensaje.txt` for `alumno@lpi.example` (output `mensaje.txt.gpg`) and decrypt it to `mensaje-recuperado.txt`.
Your terminal opens in the challenge directory (`/home/alumno/retos/r102-gpg-simetrico`); the files requested without a path go there.
lpic1-gpg-simetrico.blind_alert: REQUEST [ENCRYPTION] · Need to deliver a password-encrypted file and another encrypted for a recipient, with a separate keyring.
hints: They are two different types of encryption: one with a shared password and another with someone's public key. To make `gpg` not ask anything, batch mode is required.
Useful options: `--batch --pinentry-mode loopback --passphrase ...`, `--symmetric`, `--quick-generate-key`, `--armor --export`, `--encrypt -r`, and `-d`. Use `-o` to choose the output file.

`gpg --batch --pinentry-mode loopback --passphrase clave-reto --symmetric -o secreto.txt.gpg secreto.txt`; the key with `--quick-generate-key 'Alumno LPI <alumno@lpi.example>' default default never` (empty passphrase); then `--armor --export`, `--encrypt -r`, and `-d -o`.
lpic1-gpg-simetrico.solution_summary: Symmetric encryption uses `--symmetric` with the passphrase in loopback mode. `--quick-generate-key 'NAME <email>' default default never` creates the ed25519 key without expiry. `--armor --export` gives the public key in ASCII. `--encrypt -r email` encrypts for the recipient, and `gpg -d -o` recovers the original with the keyring's private key.

lpic1-shell-entorno3.title: A shell environment that loads automatically in every session
lpic1-shell-entorno3.briefing:
You are asked to make your environment work in any new shell. Everything must be placed in `~/.bashrc`; writing it only in the current shell will not work.
1. Create the folder `~/bin` with an executable script `saluda` that writes `hola desde ~/bin`. Add `~/bin` to the beginning of `PATH` in `~/.bashrc`.
2. Define a function `fyi` that writes three lines: the username, home directory, and hostname.
3. Define an alias `carpeta` that runs `pwd` and then `ls -la`, in that order.
To test it, open another shell with `bash` and run `saluda`, `fyi`, and `carpeta`.
Your terminal opens in the challenge directory (`/home/alumno/retos/r102-shell-entorno3`); the files requested without a path go there.
lpic1-shell-entorno3.blind_alert: REQUEST [ENVIRONMENT] · Every time you open a new shell you lose your utilities. They need to be made permanent in the user's configuration.
hints: A script is only found by name if it's in a directory on `PATH`. And what you want to persist goes in the file that `bash` reads when starting an interactive shell.
Add to `~/.bashrc` an `export PATH=...` that puts `$HOME/bin` first, a function like `name() { ...; }`, and an `alias name='cmd1; cmd2'`. For the data: `id -un`, `$HOME`, and `uname -n`.
Write in `~/.bashrc`: `export PATH="$HOME/bin:$PATH"`, `fyi() { echo ...; echo ...; echo ...; }`, and `alias carpeta='pwd; ls -la'`. Create `~/bin/saluda` with `#!/bin/bash` and run `chmod +x`.
lpic1-shell-entorno3.solution_summary: `~/.bashrc` is read in each new interactive shell, so it's where to put `export PATH="$HOME/bin:$PATH"`, the `fyi` function (with `id -un`, `$HOME`, and `uname -n`), and the alias `carpeta='pwd; ls -la'`. The `~/bin/saluda` script needs a shebang and execute permission to be found via `PATH`.

lpic1-sudo.title: Custom sudo permissions for the support user
lpic1-sudo.briefing:
You are asked to give `soporte` only two permissions with `sudo`. Create the file `/etc/sudoers.d/soporte` with these rules (use `sudo`, you are `alumno`):
1. `soporte` can run as root, without a password, `/usr/bin/ls /root` and `/usr/bin/id` (the latter with any arguments).
2. `soporte` can run `/usr/bin/whoami` as the user `www-data`, also without a password.
3. The file is owned by root and has permissions `440`.
4. Check the syntax with `sudo visudo -cf` and save its output to `visudo.txt`.
To test it: `sudo su - soporte -c 'sudo -l'`.
Your terminal opens in the challenge directory (`/home/alumno/retos/r102-sudo`); the files requested without a path go there.
lpic1-sudo.blind_alert: REQUEST [PRIVILEGES] · The user `soporte` needs two specific sudo permissions and nothing else.
hints: Each sudoers rule specifies who, from where, as which user, whether a password is required, and which commands. A file in `sudoers.d` is best edited with the tool that validates syntax.
Format: `user ALL=(target) NOPASSWD: /path/cmd args, /path/other`. For the second case you need another line with `(www-data)`. Then `chmod 440` and `visudo -cf FILE`.

Two lines: `soporte ALL=(root) NOPASSWD: /usr/bin/ls /root, /usr/bin/id` and `soporte ALL=(www-data) NOPASSWD: /usr/bin/whoami`. Save them with `sudo visudo -f /etc/sudoers.d/soporte` and redirect `sudo visudo -cf /etc/sudoers.d/soporte` to `visudo.txt`.
lpic1-sudo.solution_summary: The rules `user ALL=(target) NOPASSWD: command` limit what `soporte` can run and as whom. A command without arguments in sudoers allows any; with arguments it requires exactly those. The file must be `root:root` and `0440`, and `visudo -cf` confirms it parsed correctly.

checks.soporte puede ejecutar whoami como www-d: soporte can run whoami as www-data (and not as root)

lpic1-limites.title: Persistent resource limits for the interns group
lpic1-limites.briefing:
You are asked to limit what the interns can do. There is a group `alumnos` and a user `becario` who belongs to it.
Create the file `/etc/security/limits.d/90-alumnos.conf` (same format as `/etc/security/limits.conf`: domain, type, item, value) with these limits:
1. For the entire group `alumnos`: soft limit of locked memory (`memlock`) of 2048.
2. For the group `alumnos`: hard limit of `memlock` of 4096.
3. Only for the user `becario`: hard limit on file size (`fsize`) of 10240.
To see it: `sudo su - becario -c 'ulimit -Sl; ulimit -Hl; ulimit -Hf'`.
Your terminal opens in the challenge directory (`/home/alumno/retos/r102-limites`); the files requested without a path go there.
lpic1-limites.blind_alert: REQUEST [RESOURCES] · The interns are using more than they should. Their limits need to be set permanently.
hints: Per-user or per-group limits are applied by PAM at login, reading a config file with one line per limit. There is a `.d` directory for adding your own.
Each line is `domain type item value`. A group is written with a symbol before the name; types are `soft` and `hard`. You need `sudo` to write to `/etc/security/limits.d/`.
Three lines: `@alumnos soft memlock 2048`, `@alumnos hard memlock 4096`, and `becario hard fsize 10240`. Test with `su -`, which does open a PAM session.
lpic1-limites.solution_summary: In `limits.d` each line is `domain type item value`; the `@` prefix indicates a group. The three lines set soft and hard `memlock` for `@alumnos` and hard `fsize` for `becario`. They are applied by `pam_limits` at login, so they show up with `su -` and not in an already-open shell.

lpic1-claves-ssh.title: Key-based access: ed25519 pair, authorized_keys, and a Host entry in ssh_config
lpic1-claves-ssh.briefing:
You are asked to set up key-based access for the user `root` to the account `ina` (which already exists). You need root privileges (`sudo -i`).
1. As root, generate an ed25519 key pair without a passphrase at `/root/.ssh/lab_ed25519`, with the comment `root@lpi-lab`.
2. Create `/home/ina/.ssh` (owned by `ina`, permissions `700`) and inside it `authorized_keys` (owned by `ina`, permissions `600`) containing your public key.
3. Add to `/root/.ssh/config` a `Host servidor-lab` block with `HostName 127.0.0.1`, `User ina`, `Port 2222`, and `IdentityFile ~/.ssh/lab_ed25519`.
To view it without connecting: `ssh -G servidor-lab | grep -E '^(hostname|user|port|identityfile) '`.
Your terminal opens in the challenge directory (`/home/alumno/retos/r102-claves-ssh`); the files requested without a path go there.
lpic1-claves-ssh.blind_alert: REQUEST [SSH ACCESS] · Need to set up key-based access from `root` to the account `ina`.
hints: Three pieces: the key, who accepts it, and how the client uses it. SSH is very strict about ownership and permissions of `.ssh` and `authorized_keys`.
`ssh-keygen` has options for type (`-t`), passphrase (`-N`), comment (`-C`), and file (`-f`). `install -d -m 700 -o ina -g ina` creates the directory with owner and mode in one step.

`ssh-keygen -t ed25519 -N '' -C root@lpi-lab -f /root/.ssh/lab_ed25519`; then `cat` the `.pub` into `authorized_keys`, `chown ina:ina`, and `chmod 600`. The `Host` block goes in `/root/.ssh/config` with one option per line.
lpic1-claves-ssh.solution_summary: The private key stays in `/root/.ssh`, and the public key is added to `ina`'s `authorized_keys`, which must be owned by `ina` with mode `600` inside a `.ssh` directory with mode `700`. The `Host servidor-lab` block in `~/.ssh/config` sets alias, destination, user, port, and key; `ssh -G` shows the resulting configuration without connecting.

lpic1-xvfb.title: A virtual X server protected with an xauth cookie
lpic1-xvfb.briefing:
You are asked to start a virtual X server that draws in memory. Use display `:7`.
1. Use `xauth` to create a cookie for display `:7` in the file `cookie` (in your challenge directory).
2. Start `Xvfb` in the background on display `:7`, using that cookie (`-auth`) and a screen `0` of `800x600x24`.
3. With `DISPLAY` and `XAUTHORITY` set correctly, save the output of `xdpyinfo` to `pantalla.txt`.
Without the cookie the server must reject you: test with `XAUTHORITY=/dev/null xdpyinfo`.
Your terminal opens in the challenge directory (`/home/alumno/retos/r102-xvfb`); the files requested without a path go there.
lpic1-xvfb.blind_alert: REQUEST [GRAPHICS] · A service needs an X server without a physical display, and it must only accept authorized clients.
hints: The X server accepts only clients that present a cookie it knows. There's a tool to create that cookie in a file and environment variables so clients can find it.
`xauth -f FILE add :7 . KEY` creates the entry; `mcookie` generates a random key. The server is started with `Xvfb :7 -auth FILE -screen 0 AxBxP &`. Clients need `DISPLAY` and `XAUTHORITY`.

`xauth -f cookie add :7 . $(mcookie)`; `Xvfb :7 -auth "$PWD/cookie" -screen 0 800x600x24 &`; `export DISPLAY=:7 XAUTHORITY="$PWD/cookie"` and `xdpyinfo > pantalla.txt` (wait a moment for the server to start).
lpic1-xvfb.solution_summary: `xauth -f cookie add :7 . $(mcookie)` stores the MIT-MAGIC-COOKIE for display `:7`. `Xvfb :7 -auth cookie -screen 0 800x600x24` starts the server requiring it. With `DISPLAY=:7` and `XAUTHORITY` pointing to the cookie, `xdpyinfo` responds; without it, the server rejects it.

lpic1-localizacion.title: Date format and encoding according to locale
lpic1-localizacion.briefing:
You are asked to control the locale on a per-command basis.
1. Using the fixed date in `fecha.txt`, get the month name in English and save it to `mes.txt`.
2. Make only that command use the locale `C`.
3. Save the character encoding of the locale `C.UTF-8` to `codificacion.txt`.
Your terminal opens in the challenge directory (`/home/alumno/retos/r102-localizacion`); the files requested without a path go there.
lpic1-localizacion.blind_alert: REQUEST [LOCALE] · A report shows the month in another language. Need to control the locale for a single command.
hints: The environment variables `LC_*` and `LANG` decide language and format. They can be placed before a command to affect only that one.
`date -d` accepts a date as text and `+%B` gives the month name. To find the encoding, there's the `locale` command with an option that prints only the character set.
`LC_ALL=C date -d "$(cat fecha.txt)" +%B > mes.txt` and `LC_ALL=C.UTF-8 locale charmap > codificacion.txt`.
lpic1-localizacion.solution_summary: `LC_ALL=C` placed before a command only affects that process; `date -d "$(cat fecha.txt)" +%B` prints `January`. `locale charmap` shows the encoding of the active locale, which with `LC_ALL=C.UTF-8` is `UTF-8`.

lpic1-subredes.title: IPv4 subnets calculated by hand and verified
lpic1-subredes.briefing:
You are asked to first calculate by hand and then check with `ipcalc`. One item per line, nothing else:
1. In `red-a.txt`, for `10.0.45.200` with mask `255.255.240.0`, four lines in this order: the CIDR prefix (just the number), the network address, the broadcast address, and the number of usable hosts.
2. In `red-b.txt`, for `192.168.100.130/26`, four lines in this order: the dotted-decimal mask, the network address, the broadcast address, and the number of hosts.
3. In `binario.txt`, the address `192.168.100.130` in binary: four groups of 8 bits separated by dots.
Your terminal opens in the challenge directory (`/home/alumno/retos/r102-subredes`); the files requested without a path go there.
lpic1-subredes.blind_alert: REQUEST [ADDRESSING] · Need to document two networks: prefix, network, broadcast, and usable hosts.
hints: The prefix is the number of 1 bits in the mask. Each subnet's blocks grow by a regular amount in the octet where the boundary falls.
Usable hosts = 2^(32 - prefix) - 2. Octet bit values: 128 64 32 16 8 4 2 1. `ipcalc ADDRESS/PREFIX` shows the result for cross-checking.
With `/20` the third octet increments by 16 (network `10.0.32.0`); with `/26` the fourth by 64 (network `192.168.100.128`). Convert each octet of the address to 8 bits.
lpic1-subredes.solution_summary: A mask `255.255.240.0` is 20 bits of 1 (`/20`); the block size in the third octet is 16, so the network is `10.0.32.0`, broadcast `10.0.47.255`, and there are 4094 hosts. With `/26` the mask is `255.255.255.192`, blocks of 64: network `.128`, broadcast `.191`, 62 hosts. `ipcalc` confirms the calculations.

lpic1-puertos-ipv6.title: Ports from /etc/services and IPv6 address abbreviation
lpic1-puertos-ipv6.briefing:
You are asked to look up `/etc/services` (using `getent services` or `grep`) and abbreviate two IPv6 addresses.
1. In `puertos.txt`, one per line and in this order, the port number for: `ssh`, `smtp`, `domain` (DNS), `imaps`, and `ldaps`.
2. In `servicio.txt`, two lines: the name `/etc/services` gives to port `995/tcp` and the name for port `514/udp` (note: `514/tcp` is a different service).
3. In `ipv6.txt`, two lines with the shortest form of these addresses (`0000` groups as `0` and `::` only once):
   `fd42:abcd:1234:0000:0000:0000:0000:5678`
   `2001:dead:0000:0000:beef:0000:0000:cafe`
Your terminal opens in the challenge directory (`/home/alumno/retos/r102-puertos-ipv6`); files requested without a path go there.
lpic1-puertos-ipv6.blind_alert: REQUEST [DOCUMENTATION] · Known service ports and two IPv6 addresses must be written in their short form.
hints: `/etc/services` maps name, port, and protocol. In IPv6 you can remove leading zeros from each group and replace one run of zero groups with a double colon.
`getent services NOMBRE` or `getent services PUERTO/PROTOCOLO` query the table. `grep -w 514 /etc/services` shows you both protocols for 514.
`::` may appear only once: in the second address there are two runs of zeros and both are the same length; compressing either one is fine. The first has a single long run.
lpic1-puertos-ipv6.solution_summary: `getent services ssh` gives 22/tcp, `smtp` 25, `domain` 53, `imaps` 993, and `ldaps` 636. Port 995/tcp is `pop3s` and 514/udp is `syslog`. In IPv6, `fd42:abcd:1234::5678` compresses the single run; in the second address, compress one run of zeros and write the others as `0`.

lpic1-resolucion.title: Name resolution order, lab hosts, and search domain
lpic1-resolucion.briefing:
Someone changed how this machine resolves names and two lab servers are missing. You are asked to:
1. Fix `/etc/nsswitch.conf`: the `hosts` line must check local files (`files`) first and then DNS (`dns`).
2. Add two machines to `/etc/hosts`, each with its fully qualified name and short alias: `192.168.50.10` `servidor.lab.local` (alias `servidor`) and `192.168.50.20` `backup.lab.local` (alias `backup`).
3. Save the output of `getent hosts backup` in `backup.txt`.
4. In `/etc/resolv.conf`, add the domain `lab.local` to the search list (`search`) without removing existing ones and WITHOUT touching the `nameserver` lines. Note: the container mounts this file, so `sed -i` doesn't work; use an editor or `>>`.
You need `sudo` to edit these files.
Your terminal opens in the challenge directory (`/home/alumno/retos/r102-resolucion`); files requested without a path go there.
lpic1-resolucion.blind_alert: INCIDENT [RESOLUTION] · Lab names don't resolve as they should since someone touched the client configuration.
hints: There are three separate pieces: the order of name sources, the local table, and the search domains of the DNS client. `getent` queries just like any application would.

Look at the `hosts` line in `/etc/nsswitch.conf`. In `/etc/hosts` each line is IP, fully qualified name, and alias. In `resolv.conf` only the last `search` line counts. Edit with `sudo nano` or use `sudo tee -a`.

Set `hosts: files dns`. Add `192.168.50.10 servidor.lab.local servidor` and `192.168.50.20 backup.lab.local backup`. Add a `search` line at the end of `resolv.conf` with the domains that were already there plus `lab.local`.
lpic1-resolucion.solution_summary: `nsswitch.conf` had `dns files`; it must be `hosts: files dns` so the local table wins. In `/etc/hosts` the format is `IP nombre-completo alias`. In `resolv.conf` only the last `search` line matters, so repeat it with the previous domains plus `lab.local` without touching the `nameserver` lines.

lpic1-networkd.title: Laptop networking with systemd-networkd .network files and WPA
lpic1-networkd.briefing:
You are asked to write out the network configuration for a laptop. There is no systemd in the container, so you only create the files (use `sudo`):
1. `/etc/systemd/network/30-lan.network`: must apply to ALL ethernet interfaces (using a wildcard), with static IP `192.168.0.100/24`, gateway `192.168.0.1`, and DNS server `192.168.0.1`.
2. `/etc/systemd/network/40-wifi.network`: for the `wlo1` interface, request only the IPv4 address via DHCP.
3. Using `wpa_passphrase`, create `/etc/wpa_supplicant/wpa_supplicant-wlo1.conf` for the network `MyWifi` with the password `MyPassword`. Then delete the commented line from that file that contains the clear-text password.
4. Save in `servicio.txt` the full name of the systemd unit that file would use to connect `wlo1`.

lpic1-ip-rutas.title: Reading interfaces, default route, and addresses with ip

lpic1-ss-nc.title: Locating a hidden service with ss and talking to it with nc

While setting up the challenge, a TCP service was started that listens only on `127.0.0.1`, on a high port between `20000` and `29999` that we won't tell you. You are asked to:
1. Find it with `ss` and save the port number in `puerto.txt`.
2. Save in `programa.txt` the name of the program listening on that port.
3. Connect with `nc`: it replies with a sentence ending in a key word. Save only that word in `clave.txt`.
4. Stop the service with `kill` and verify with `ss` that it is no longer listening.
The service runs as root: to see its process and stop it you need `sudo`.
Your terminal opens in the challenge directory (`/home/alumno/retos/r102-ss-nc`); files requested without a path go there.
lpic1-ss-nc.blind_alert: INCIDENT [UNKNOWN SERVICE] · A process listens on an undocumented high local port. It must be identified and stopped.
hints: A listening service is a TCP socket in LISTEN state. `ss` lists them and can show which process owns each one, but you can see other users' processes only if you have privileges.
Use `sudo ss` with the TCP, listening, numeric, and process options. You'll see something like `users:(("nombre",pid=N,…))`. To talk to the port, use `nc 127.0.0.1 PUERTO`.
`sudo ss -tlnp` and look for the port between 20000 and 29999 on `127.0.0.1`. Connect with `nc 127.0.0.1 PUERTO < /dev/null`, take the last word of the reply, and stop the PID with `sudo kill`.

lpic1-script.title: A script with arguments, a condition, and exit codes
lpic1-script.briefing:
You are asked to write `cuenta.sh` (executable) in your challenge directory, with this behavior:
1. If it receives no arguments, it writes `uso: cuenta.sh FICHERO...` and exits with code 1.
2. If it receives arguments, it writes how many there are (just the number) and exits with code 0.
Example: `./cuenta.sh a b c` writes `3`.
Your terminal opens in the challenge directory (`/home/alumno/retos/r102-script`); files requested without a path go there.
lpic1-script.blind_alert: REQUEST [AUTOMATION] · A utility that counts arguments and warns when none are received is missing.
hints: A script needs to say which interpreter runs it and have execute permission. The shell stores the number of arguments in a special variable.
`$#` is the number of arguments. Use `if [ ... ]; then ... fi` for the no-arguments case, and `exit` with the appropriate code.
First line `#!/bin/bash`; `if [ $# -eq 0 ]; then echo 'uso: cuenta.sh FICHERO...'; exit 1; fi`; then `echo $#`. Finish with `chmod +x cuenta.sh`.
lpic1-script.solution_summary: The shebang `#!/bin/bash` selects the interpreter and `chmod +x` makes it executable. `$#` counts the arguments: with 0 the usage message is printed and it exits with `exit 1`; otherwise `echo $#` prints the total and the script ends with 0.

lpic1-usuarios.title: Creating a user with a group, expiration, and locked password

hints: There are four account operations, each with its own command: groups, users, expiration, and locking. All require privileges.
`useradd` has options to create the home directory, set the shell, and add secondary groups. Expiration is managed with `chage`; locking, with `passwd` or `usermod`.
`sudo groupadd desarrollo`; `sudo useradd -m -s /bin/bash -G desarrollo ana`; `sudo chage -E 2027-12-31 ana`; `sudo passwd -l ana`.

lpic1-suid.title: SUID file audit
lpic1-suid.briefing:
An auditor asks you for two things:

lpic1-zonahoraria.title: Time zone without timedatectl and dates with date
lpic1-zonahoraria.briefing:
The container has no `timedatectl` (no systemd), so you'll do it by hand. You need `sudo`:
1. Change the system time zone to `America/Bogota`: `/etc/localtime` must be a symbolic link to its file under `/usr/share/zoneinfo`.
2. Without changing the system zone, save to `tokio.txt` the abbreviation of the `Asia/Tokyo` zone (the one given by `date +%Z`, with the `TZ` variable set only for that command).
3. Save to `epoch.txt` the UTC date, in `YYYY-MM-DD` format, of the instant `1564013011` (seconds since the epoch).

hints: The system zone is a link to a file in the time zone database. An environment variable lets you test another zone without touching the system.

`sudo ln -sf /usr/share/zoneinfo/America/Bogota /etc/localtime`; `TZ=Asia/Tokyo date +%Z > tokio.txt`; `date -u -d @1564013011 +%F > epoch.txt`.
lpic1-zonahoraria.solution_summary: `/etc/localtime` is a link to `/usr/share/zoneinfo/America/Bogota`, which `ln -sf` replaces. `TZ=Asia/Tokyo date +%Z` applies the zone only to that command and returns `JST`. `date -u -d @1564013011 +%F` converts the epoch to a UTC date (2019-07-25).

lpic1-rsyslog.title: rsyslog rules for application logs
lpic1-rsyslog.briefing:
Your application logs with the `local5` facility. The `rsyslogd` daemon is stopped at the start. You are asked (with `sudo`):
1. Create `/etc/rsyslog.d/60-app.conf` with two rules: all `local5` messages to `/var/log/app.log`, and only those with priority exactly `err` from `local5` to `/var/log/app-err.log`.
2. Check the syntax with `rsyslogd -N1` and start `rsyslogd` by hand (the container has no `systemctl`).
3. Using `logger` and the `app` tag, send three `local5` messages: `arranque correcto` with priority `info`, `fallo de disco` with `err`, and `temperatura alta` with `crit`.

Create `/etc/logrotate.d/tienda` for `/var/log/tienda/*.log` with: weekly rotation, 4 copies, compression delayed one cycle (`compress` and `delaycompress`), don't fail if the file is missing, don't rotate empty files, and create the new file with `640` permissions, owner `root`, and group `adm`.

hints: A `logrotate.d` file is a block with the log path and one directive per line. There are options for frequency, number of copies, compression, and permissions of the new file.

lpic1-diario.title: Querying another machine's journal copy with journalctl
lpic1-diario.briefing:
In `diario/` you have a copy of the systemd journal from machine `web01`. Read it with `journalctl -D diario` (without touching the container journal) and save only the message text, one per line (`-o cat`):
1. In `errores.txt`, the messages from the `copias` tag with priority `err` or more severe.
2. In `avisos.txt`, messages from any tag with priority exactly `warning` (neither more nor less severe).
3. In `ultimas.txt`, the 3 most recent entries from `sshd`, starting with the newest.
Your terminal opens in the challenge directory (`/home/alumno/retos/r102-diario`); files requested without a path go there.
lpic1-diario.blind_alert: REQUEST [DIAGNOSTICS] · The systemd journal from `web01` has been brought and three specific listings must be extracted.
hints: `journalctl` can read another journal directory and filter by tag, priority and order. With a simple output format you'll only see the text.
`-D DIR` selects the journal, `-t ETIQUETA` filters by identifier, `-p` by priority (it supports a `desde..hasta` range), `-r` reverses the order and `-n N` limits the number of lines.

hints: Aliases are a text table that the MTA queries from a binary database; editing the text is not enough. Personal forwarding is a file in each user's home.
Format: `nombre: destino1, destino2`. To rebuild the database there is a command that starts with `new`. The `.forward` only contains the destination address.
Add `soporte: marta, pablo` and `webmaster: root` to `/etc/aliases`, run `sudo newaliases`, and as `pablo`, `echo marta > ~/.forward`.
lpic1-aliases.solution_summary: Each alias is `nombre: destinos` in `/etc/aliases`. `newaliases` regenerates `aliases.db` so Postfix reads it. `pablo`'s `~/.forward` contains `marta` and redirects their mail; it must belong to `pablo`.

checks.la base de alias ya conoce webmaster: the alias database already knows webmaster
checks./home/pablo/.forward es de pablo y reenv: /home/pablo/.forward is pablo's and forwards to marta

lpic1-ssh-claves.title: SSH keys for alumno, strict permissions, and configuration block
lpic1-ssh-claves.briefing:
They ask you to prepare SSH for your user `alumno`, which starts with an empty `~/.ssh`:
1. In `/home/alumno/.ssh`, generate an ed25519 key pair called `id_ed25519`, without a passphrase.
2. Set the strict permissions SSH requires: `/home/alumno/.ssh` with `700` and the private key `id_ed25519` with `600`.
3. Copy the contents of `id_ed25519.pub` to `/home/alumno/.ssh/authorized_keys` and give it `600` permissions.
4. Create `/home/alumno/.ssh/config` with `600` permissions and a block for host `servidor-lab` with `HostName 10.0.0.50`, `User operador`, and `Port 2222`.
Your terminal opens in the challenge directory (`/home/alumno/retos/r102-ssh-claves`); files requested without a path go there.
lpic1-ssh-claves.blind_alert: REQUEST [SSH ACCESS] · The keys for `alumno` must be left ready with the permissions SSH requires and a shortcut to the lab server.
hints: SSH rejects keys and files with permissions that are too open. There are four pieces: the key pair, the folder, who can get in, and the client shortcut.
`ssh-keygen` takes the type, passphrase and output file via options. In `config` each block starts with `Host` and its options go below, one per line.

`ssh-keygen -t ed25519 -N "" -f ~/.ssh/id_ed25519`; `chmod 700 ~/.ssh`; `chmod 600` on the private key, on `authorized_keys` and on `config`; the block has `Host servidor-lab`, `HostName`, `User` and `Port`.
lpic1-ssh-claves.solution_summary: `ssh-keygen -t ed25519 -N "" -f …/id_ed25519` creates the pair. SSH requires `700` on `.ssh` and `600` on the private key, on `authorized_keys` and on `config`. The public key copied to `authorized_keys` allows access with that key, and the `Host servidor-lab` block defines destination, user, and port.

checks.clave pública id_ed25519.pub es de tipo: public key id_ed25519.pub is of type ed25519
checks.authorized_keys contiene la clave públic: authorized_keys contains the public key and has permissions 600
checks.config define el host servidor-lab con H: config defines host servidor-lab with HostName, User, and Port
checks.~/.ssh y sus ficheros son de alumno (no: ~/.ssh and its files belong to alumno (not root)
